hints: Look first at carbon 1 on the right side of each ring and compare where its OH group points compared to the CH2OH group at the top.
Remember beta-glucose has the C1 OH and the CH2OH on the same side (both up), and all the other OH groups must also match the glucose pattern, not the galactose pattern.
walkthrough:
**Spot the anomeric carbon**

Look at carbon 1, the carbon on the right of the ring next to the O. This is the carbon that decides alpha or beta. Focus on whether its OH is up or down relative to the CH2OH group at the top.

Rule to remember: $CH_2OH$ up + C1 $OH$ up = beta, $CH_2OH$ up + C1 $OH$ down = alpha.

**Sort alpha from beta**

In A and C the C1 OH points down while CH2OH points up, so they are alpha forms. In B and D the C1 OH points up with CH2OH up, so they are beta forms. This narrows the answer to B or D.

**Check it is glucose, not another hexose**

Glucose and galactose both have formula $C_6H_{12}O_6$ but differ at carbon 4. In glucose the pattern of OH groups fits B exactly. In D the OH on one of the lower carbons is flipped to the opposite side, so D is a different sugar (a beta-galactose type structure). Therefore only B shows beta-glucose.

options.A: Shows alpha-glucose because the C1 OH points down while CH2OH points up, the opposite sides.
options.B: Shows beta-glucose because both CH2OH and the C1 OH point up on the same side, with all other OH groups in the glucose positions.
options.C: Shows an alpha form with C1 OH down, and the lower OH pattern is also different from glucose.
options.D: Shows a beta C1 position with OH up, but one of the other OH groups is flipped, so it is not glucose.
